newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW-Mexico's TFM aims for truck market share.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Mexico's TFM aims for truck market share.

text.p: Mexican railroad operator Transportacion Ferroviaria Mexicana (TFM) is looking to compete for the cargo market share currently dominated in Mexico by truckers, TFM executive vice-president Brad Skinner said.

"We've identified with our customers a possible conversion of 17 million tonnes, a 70 percent increase from the current (annual) 22 million tonnes of cargo on the line," Skinner told Reuters in an interview late Monday.
Garnering that business would take TFM cargo traffic up to 39 million tonnes per year.
Skinner said cargo on the network should grow at a rate of up to 20 percent per year for "at least the next five years.".
The company, a joint venture between Transportacion Maritima Mexicana (TMM) and Kansas City Southern Industries, took control of the Northeast Railroad on Monday.
The Northeast line carries 60 percent of Mexico's grain imports and 90 percent of movements of vehicle and autopart imports.

It is considered the jewel of the country's railway system which the government is privatizing section-by-section in a bid to modernize the country's tracks, which have not seen substantial development or investment for decades.
The route connects the key ports of Manzanillo, Tampico, Veracruz and Lazaro Cardenas with U.S. border sites Nuevo Laredo and Matamoros and industrial centers Saltillo, Monterrey and Mexico City.

Skinner said TFM aims to steer clients away from using trucks by making rail transport a more reliable and secure option. He claimed railway transportation is between 30 to 50 percent cheaper than transport by trucks.
TFM conducted a poll of 169 clients, and concluded that reliability, a set schedule, customer service and security were the top demands, he said.
"If we do these things we will be able to convert a lot of cargo from truckers," Skinner said.
The company has ambitious plans for the rail network, and dubs it the "southern half" of a North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) freeway that interconnects Canada, the United States and Mexico.

Skinner said TFM plans to spend $107 million to purchase equipment for the line in 1997 including equipment from new locomotives to computer systems. TMM chair Jose Serrano has said the venture will invest $800 million on the route in the next five years.
TFM's capital expenditures are meant to reverse decades of inefficiencies inherited from the former government-operation of the railroad.

"TFM faces significant challenges as they embark in the turnaround of a transportation mode that has been so inefficient and labor-bloated up to now that it has lost significant market share to other forms of freight transportation, primarily trucking, despite higher trucking rates," Bear Stearns analyst Sandy Pique wrote.

To reverse what analysts called a highly overstaffed operation, TFM cut about half of the railroad's work force. The railway's workers, about 8,500 in 1995, were laid off when the railway was privatized and TFM plans to hire back between 3,600 to 4,000 workers, Skinner said.

"They have to turn around a line that has been very abandoned, demonstrate that it is worth what they offered for it," Pique added. "They never gave a convincing response as to why they offered so much."

TFM paid $1.4 billion for a 50-year concession, almost three times the nearest bid for the route. The government later stepped in and took back a 33.5 stake, saying TFM approached them with financing problems.
